stories.headline: Dream rule out top scorer Allisha Gray (finger) for Game 2
stories.summary: Dream guard Allisha Gray was ruled out of Game 2 of their semifinal series against the Liberty because of a finger injury and is considered day-to-day.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- Atlanta Dream guard Allisha Gray was ruled out of Wednesday's Game 2 of their semifinal series against the New York Liberty because of a finger injury and is considered day-to-day, coach Karl Smesko told reporters on Tuesday.

Gray had an X-ray on her finger, though Smesko did not share any additional info on the nature or severity of her injury. Guard Rhyne Howard characterized the update as "good news."

Smesko said he anticipates Gray -- who was not present at practice Tuesday -- to be with the team for Wednesday's game, and teammates said she was in good spirits.

"Nobody's going to try to be Lish because, I mean, there's only one Lish," Smesko said. "Lish is one of the best players in the league. She's an exceptional scorer and she's an excellent defender. So being without her for a game is tough, but we have players that are ready to step up.

"It's not who you don't have; it's how well do the players who are on the floor, how well are they able to execute the game plan, and how well are they able to play? And I expect our team to play really well."

Gray exited Sunday's 92-82 Game 1 win at the end of the first quarter because of a left, shooting hand injury before returning in the second and then reinjuring it. She was ruled out for the remainder of the game shortly before halftime, scoring seven points in her 11 minutes on the floor.

The 6-foot guard and four-time All-Star out of South Carolina was the Dream's top scorer this season, averaging 19.0 points, 3.5 rebounds, 2.6 assists and 1.4 steals while appearing in all 44 contests. She was also their top scorer (22.0 PPG) during a first-round sweep of the No. 5 seed Washington Mystics as Atlanta secured its first semifinals berth since 2018.

"Obviously knowing that Lish will be out, it hurts, it sucks," forward Naz Hillmon said. "I know how much she would want to be on the floor with us. We know how much we use her offensively and defensively. But that next woman up mentality is for everybody. Not just the players coming off the bench or whoever's going to fill in her role, nobody's going to be able to do what Allisha Gray does.

"We all know that, but we can all put a little bit more on our plate, and that's what our mentality is."

stories.headline: AFL player movement tracker: trade requests, free agency latest, who's on the move?
stories.summary: The offseason is upon us which means AFL trades, free agency, and player movement is about to take off. Here's the latest news, whispers, and confirmed deals.
stories.body:
It's AFL player movement season, with trades and free agency set to dominate the month of October. So who is going where? Keep track with our player movement guide here.

When is the AFL trade and free agency window?
The 2026 AFL trade period commences on Monday, October 5 and closes in the evening of Wednesday, October 14.

The free agency window opens and closes a little earlier; it runs from Friday, October 2 until Friday, October 9.

Tuesday, Oct. 6
O'Driscoll makes the move over east

Fremantle have traded 24-year-old Nathan O'Driscoll to Richmond in exchange for pick 61 in this year's draft.

The winger played 17 games for the Dockers this season but wasn't selected for the Grand Final.

Monday, Oct. 5
TRADE PERIOD OPENS
Merrett finally becomes a Hawk

After attempting to join Hawthorn last year, Zach Merrett has finally been traded from Essendon to the Hawks.

Hawthorn have sent picks 15, 25 and a 2028 second-round pick in exchange for the 31-year-old.

Merrett leaves the Bombers a week after winning a record-equaling seventh Crichton Medal, three All-Australian blazers, and 274 games.

Pendlebury becomes a Sun

AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury is officially a Sun after Gold Coast and Collingwood agreed on a trade for the 38-year-old veteran.

Pendlebury, a two-time premiership player, heads to the Suns in exchange for pick No. 65 in this year's draft.

"It's an exciting group here at the SUNS and the opportunity to bring a few different ideas and also learn from a great group of coaches and players is one I'm really looking forward to," Pendlebury told the Suns.

"This side is one I've watched from afar and really admired. I've got a bit of knowledge about the industry so I'm here to play my role and help this squad continue to develop."

Jesse Hogan traded from GWS to Collingwood

Out-of-favour Giants forward Jesse Hogan has made the switch to Collingwood in exchange for pick 75.

The 31-year-old won the Coleman Medal in 2024 but has been unable to recapture his best form at the Giants in the two years since.

Magpies list boss Justin Leppitsch said Hogan would be a valuable addition.

"On behalf of everyone at Collingwood, I'd like to warmly welcome Jesse to Collingwood. Jesse has established himself as one of the competition's premier key forwards and we're excited to see him bring his experience and talent to our club," he said.

"His aerial presence inside forward-50 and his consistency as a goal-kicker make him a genuine threat.

"Like Lachie (Neale), Jesse has a passion to teach the next generation and will make a great addition to our club."

Saturday, Oct. 3
Bulldogs seal free-agency signing of key defender

The Western Bulldogs have finally snagged the key defender they need, securing Adelaide backman Jordon Butts as an unrestricted free agent.

The Bulldogs are set for a bumper AFL trade period headlined by working through a deal for Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, ahead of a 2027 season where the club will have high expectations.

But after seeing off Carlton's advances to keep hold of defender Buku Khamis, the Bulldogs have filled a major area of need by adding 26-year-old Butts.

Adelaide will receive a second-round compensation selection, currently pick No.33, in this year's draft.

-- AAP

Friday, Oct. 2
FREE AGENCY OPEN
Three-peat Lion locks in Magpies move

Lachie Neale has sealed his high-profile switch to Collingwood, with Brisbane teasing the dual Brownlow medallist on his way out the door.

The AFL approved Neale signing a three-year deal with the Magpies on Friday afternoon, closing out the first day of free agency.

The 33-year-old ball-winner leaves as an unrestricted free agent after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with their stunning seven-point grand final victory over Fremantle.

-- AAP

Greene on his way to the Cats

Toby Greene will join Geelong as an unrestricted free agent on a three-year deal, re-partnering with former Giants teammate Jeremey Cameron.

The paperwork was lodged to the AFL on Friday morning.

The Giants receive band three compensation for Greene, which is currently pick No. 26 in the upcoming draft.

Greene departs the Giants with his name etched in the club's record books, sitting first in games played for the club with a tally of 282 games, as well as leading the club's all-time goalkicking tally with 450 majors.

Briggs now a Tiger

Richmond has landed GWS ruck Kieren Briggs as an unrestricted free agent.

Briggs' move to the Tigers was confirmed just hours after the free agency window opened on Friday.

Briggs played 88 games for GWS after joining the club as the No.34 pick in the 2018 draft.

Amartey officially joins the Blues

Free agency has opened with a bang, with out-of-favour key forward Joel Amartey committing to Carlton.

Details are still to come on the length of contract, and Sydney's compensation.

Hawthorn father-son recommits despite interest

Calsher Dear has made a shock decision to re-sign with the Hawks for two years, despite being out of favour thorughout 2026.

The 20-year-old has kicked 39 goals from 31 games, but found himself behind Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis and Mabior Chol. With Gunston signed on and Suns forward Ben King expected to sign with the Hawks as well, there were questions about whether Dear would get enough opportunity at his childhood club.

Hawks list boss Mark McKenzie said the club was "really pleased" that Dear had recommitted.

"He remains an important part of what we are trying to achieve as a club," he said.

"Following his debut season, Calsher showed us all the special talent that he is, but as a key tall at 21 years of age, we've needed to be patient with his progression.

"Having battled several injuries over his first three seasons in the system, we are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond."

Thursday, Oct. 1
Goater set to make cross-city switch

North Melbourne defender Josh Goater is set to join the Hawks after requesting a trade on Thursday.

Having played just 18 games, the 23-year-old had fallen out of favour after an injury-hit run in his time at North.

Premiership Lion requests trade

The Brisbane Lions have confirmed Sam Marshall has requested a trade to St Kilda.

"The Brisbane Lions confirm premiership midfielder Sam Marshall has requested to be traded to St Kilda," the Lions said in a statement.

"Marshall has played 13 games, including the 2025 Premiership, across two seasons since being selected in the first round of the 2024 draft as a graduate of the Youi Brisbane Lions Academy.

"The club respects Marshall's request to be traded, and will work towards facilitating an outcome that best reflects true value to the Brisbane Lions for the 20-year-old."

Tuesday, Sept. 29
Neale informs Lions he intends to join Collingwood

Two-time Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale has told Brisbane he will depart the club as an unrestricted free agent and sign a three-year deal with Collingwood.

Aware that Neale intended to leave at the end of the year, the Lions never offered him a new contract.

The paperwork for the deal is expected to be formalised as early as Friday when the free agency period opens.

Friday, Sept. 25
Jordon Butts to join the Bulldogs

Zak Butters isn't the only South Australian-based player keen to join the Western Bulldogs, with Crows' key defender Jordon Butts officially naming the Dogs as his preferred offseason destination.

The unrestricted free agent will sign a five-year deal at the Kennel, according to AFL.com.au.

Tuesday, Sept. 22
Amartey officially names Carlton

Wantaway Sydney forward Joel Amartey has confirmed his desire to join Carlton as an unrestricted free agent.

The 26-year-old was kept out of the Swans' side with an Achilles injury in the latter stages of the year.

With Charlie Curnow (75 goals in 2026) and Logan McDonald (51) cementing their spots in the Sydney forward line as the prime targets, Amartey is hoping for more opportunity at the Blues.

Thursday, Sept. 17
GWS captain finally makes big call on his future

Toby Greene has opted to leave GWS, telling the AFL club he wishes to play with Geelong next season. Greene, who has been at the Giants since their foundation season in 2012, wants to go back to Victoria for family reasons.

In an extraordinary way to announce the decision, outgoing GWS boss Dave Matthews confirmed Greene's intentions on radio, before the club released a statement.

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join the Cats.

Saturday, Sept. 12
Zak Butters makes huge free agency call
The year's hottest restricted free agent Zak Butters has made a huge call on his future, nominating the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination.

After a year of speculation, with Geelong thought to be the front-runner for the Power star's signature, Butters made the call on Saturday, first reported by AFL.com.au's Callum Twomey.

The deal is reportedly for nine years.

Thursday, Sept. 10
Hogan set to join Pies
GWS and Collingwood have both confirmed that 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan has chosen the Magpies at his next home.

Set to be a four-club player, Hogan is 31 and coming off a 12-goal season from just nine appearances.

It's a big boost for the Magpies if Hogan can recapture his form; key forward has been an area of concern for a number of years.

Tuesday, Sept. 8
Bailey set to be Lion for life
Brisbane's Zac Bailey has ended months of 'will he, won't he' speculation to sign with the Lions for eight years, taking him through the 2034 season, the the club confirmed on Tuesday.

Bailey, a free agent, had been a big target for the Crows, who had reportedly tabled a more lucrative offer.

"I'm absolutely rapt to be staying at the Brisbane Lions," Bailey said in a statement.

"I love the environment here, the players, coaches and staff who all make it a great place to be and I feel like this Club continues to bring the best out of me.

"This Club means so much to me - I came here as a young player and have grown up here and to know I will be here long-term is something I'm really proud of.

"I would like to thank the club, my partner Em, my family and my management for being so supportive throughout this process.

"I love what we as a club have achieved during my time here and I am super excited about what we can continue to achieve together."

Rowan Marshall requests trade
St Kilda ruck Rowan Marshall looks set to be on the move, with the Saints confirming the big man had requested a trade for the second straight season.

While Marshall hasn't requested a specific club, it's likely to be Geelong after he failed to secure a trade to the Cats last year. He played 21 games for the Saints this seaosn, juggling ruck duties with Tom De Koning, who came in from Carlton last offseason.

"Rowan is a highly valued member of the St Kilda Football Club and remains contracted until the end of 2027," the Saints said in a statement.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club."

Zane Duursma wants to go to Melbourne
The No. 4 pick in the 2023 AFL draft Zane Duursma has requested a trade out of North Melbourne, with Melbourne in his sights.

The news comes a week after coach Alastair Clarkson was sacked by the club. North won nine games in 2026, their best return since 2019.

Ed Allan re-signs with the Pies
After speculation about his future at the Magpies, mdifielder Ed Allan has put pen to paper, signing a four year extension to remain at Collingwood.

2026 was a breakout season for Allan, who played 19 games and averaged a career-high 16.5 disposals per game.

Monday, Sept. 7
Pair of in-demand Dogs re-sign
According to afl.com.au, both Arty Jones and Buku Khamis will remain at the Kennel this offseason.

Jones will sign a three-year deal, while Khamis has a five-year contract in front of him.

Essendon and Brisbane had interest in livewire forward Jones, who had a standout performance against Collingwood in the wildcard final win, while the Blues were heavily linked to Khamis for a second straight offseason.

Cooper Hodge nomintes Hawthorn
A big boost for the Hawks, with club champion Luke Hodge's son Cooper choosing to join the Melbourne-based team as a father-son at this year's draft.

He had the option of going to Brisbane as a Lions academy member.

stories.headline: Fantasy football buzz: Revitalizing offense just got harder for Jalen Hurts
stories.summary: Jalen Hurts and the Eagles' offense will have an even more difficult time righting the ship without RT Lane Johnson.
stories.body:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values in fantasy football.

Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

Oct. 6: Jalen Hurts' job gets a lot tougher with Lane Johnson retirement
By Michael F. Florio

Lane Johnson announced his retirement from the NFL on Tuesday. That will leave a massive hole on the offensive line for an Eagles team that is missing a ton of star players. Saquon Barkley hurt a hamstring, and he is expected to miss Week 5. DeVonta Smith was out last week due to a hamstring injury, and he seems unlikely for Week 5. And Dallas Goedert remains sidelined with a knee injury.

Jalen Hurts has struggled in games without Johnson, having averaged 174 passing yards and 1.1 passing touchdowns per game when Johnson sat. On top of that, the quarterback faces a Jacksonville Jaguars team that has allowed three passing touchdowns and has six interceptions this season. Jacksonville can get after the QB, as well, producing 10 sacks through four weeks, eighth most in the NFL. That's problematic without Johnson.

Perhaps Hurts' rushing ability saves the day, but he has not ran as much this season. He has fewer than 20 rushing yards in two of his past three games and one rushing touchdown this campaign. Plus, the Jaguars have allowed the second-fewest rushing yards and just two rushing touchdowns so far in 2026.

Some QBs I would play over Hurts are Matthew Stafford, Jacoby Brissett, Kyler Murray and Jordan Love. The "floors" here are not safe, but Jameis Winston and Aaron Rodgers are upside options this week in favorable matchups.

Falcons' offense has come alive under Michael Penix Jr.

By Michael F. Florio

The Atlanta Falcons are hitting their stride with Michael Penix Jr. They scored 45 points Monday night against the New Orleans Saints and have 80 total in Penix's two starts. Penix threw for 223 yards and one touchdown, finishing with 12.72 fantasy points. He has yet to crack 15 and is primarily a superflex option, although all the QB injuries could change that.

Penix's impact on the Falcons offense cannot be overstated. Bijan Robinson went for 147 total yards and two touchdowns Monday, and in 16 career games with Penix at the helm he has 2,181 scrimmage yards and 17 touchdowns. Robinson saves his best for primetime, which means fantasy managers are in luck, as the Falcons play the Baltimore Ravens on "Sunday Night Football" next week.

Penix also continues to elevate Drake London. After going for 194 yards in Week 3, London was held to a modest 96 yards on five catches Monday. He has 105 catches, 1,576 yards and nine touchdowns in 16 career games with Penix. He has to be viewed as an elite fantasy option as long as Penix is healthy.

And Brian Robinson Jr. had himself a night, turning 15 opportunities into 67 yards and three touchdowns. He has double-digit touches in each of his past three games and has four total touchdowns in the past two games. Robinson should be added off the waiver wire if he is out there. Not only is he one of the top insurance backs, but he is carving out a role with standalone value. He can be a flex option with byes coming up and due to all the injuries.

What else you need to know from 'Monday Night Football':

Chris Olave continues to produce at an extremely high level. He turned 12 targets into eight catches for 116 yards Monday and has topped 19 fantasy points in every game. Outside of Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Amon-Ra St. Brown, there are not many receivers I would rather have.
It was a tough game for Tyler Shough, who was able to salvage his fantasy night with a last-drive touchdown pass. He finished with 286 yards and the touchdown, failing to top 22 fantasy points for the first time this season (15.94). Still, Shough is in play outside of the tough matchups. But he has just that next week against the Minnesota Vikings, so fantasy managers may want to look at their other options.
Alvin Kamara led the way in the backfield for the Saints with 41% of the snaps, posting seven carries and seven targets. He turned those into 58 yards and two touchdowns. While it is tough to bank on big yardage from Kamara, the pass-game work paired with goal-line usage keeps him in play as a RB2 or flex option.
Juwan Johnson and Devaughn Vele continue to produce for the Saints. Johnson turned eight targets into six catches for 59 yards. He has double-digit fantasy points in every game and is the TE3 on the season. He has earned his way into starting lineups weekly. Vele finished with six catches, 54 yards and a touchdown on nine targets. He has topped 11 fantasy points three times. Vele is a high-floor option who can be started most weeks until rookie Jordyn Tyson returns.
Kendre Miller fumbled and the Saints turned to rookie CJ Donaldson late. While Kamara is the only Saints RB you can use for fantasy right now, this RB2 battle is one to monitor moving forward.

Oct. 5: Who did -- or didn't -- get the ball Sunday?

The box score doesn't tell you everything. Here are the roles and usage trends from Sunday that stood out to me.

By Eric Moody

Indianapolis Colts vs. Washington Commanders

Rachaad White's shoulder injury gave Jacory Croskey-Merritt a chance to take control of the backfield, but that didn't happen. He finished with 11 touches for 50 total yards and 7.0 fantasy points. Austin Ekeler got more involved as the game went on, finishing with five touches for 40 yards and 5.0 points while splitting early-down snaps with Croskey-Merritt in the second half. Ekeler is worth adding in deeper leagues, while Croskey-Merritt is tougher to trust. Kaytron Allen had just three touches for one yard, with Ekeler and Craig Reynolds both playing ahead of him.

New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills

James Cook III finished with 14 touches and 16.3 fantasy points against the Patriots, but it's worth noting that he set a season-low snap total. Ty Johnson continues to handle much of the passing-game and third-down work. This game was never separated by more than one score, so Cook finishing with only 14 touches is worth monitoring. He remains an RB1, but fantasy managers should keep an eye on his usage.

Rhamondre Stevenson left late with a right knee injury, but he was able to walk off under his own power. Before that, he remained the more valuable fantasy back in New England's rotation. Stevenson finished with 16 touches and 18.4 fantasy points, while TreVeyon Henderson had 14 touches for 42 yards and 4.2 points. Stevenson also continued to get the more valuable third-down, two-minute, short-yardage and goal-line work, while leading the Patriots' backfield in snaps, routes, touches and fantasy points.

New York Jets at Chicago Bears

Braelon Allen handled nearly all of the work with Breece Hall out. He played 93% of the Jets' offensive snaps, took all 14 carries and caught both of his targets. Isaiah Davis played just two snaps and didn't get a touch. The fantasy production wasn't huge, but the usage was exactly what managers wanted to see. If Hall remains out, Allen should continue to handle the bulk of the backfield work. It's worth noting that the Jets possessed the ball for just 17:15, their lowest time of possession in a game since Week 16 of the 2005 season, which helps explain why Allen's final touch total wasn't higher.

Kenyon Sadiq was held without a catch, but he did see four targets. More importantly, his snap rate and route participation both increased from Week 3 to Week 4. That's encouraging considering the Jets' low time of possession. It's also worth noting that none of Sadiq's targets were catchable. Looking ahead, the Jets face a Browns defense in Week 5 that has allowed the eighth-most receiving yards to tight ends. Sadiq remains a must-hold player.

Kyle Monangai took over after D'Andre Swift lost a fumble and finished with 30 carries, two touchdowns and 28.0 fantasy points. Swift still handled 15 carries before the benching, so Chicago's backfield remains a committee for now. Monangai's workload shows the upside if Swift misses time or loses more work. Swift remains an RB2, while Monangai is a flex with upside and would move into the RB1 conversation if he became the lead back. It's also worth noting that the Bears possessed the ball for 42:45, their highest time of possession in a game since 1994, which helped create an unusually large number of rushing attempts.

Jacksonville Jaguars at Cincinnati Bengals

Chase Brown continued to dominate Cincinnati's backfield, playing a season-high share of the snaps and finishing with 20 touches and a season-high 19.1 fantasy points. He managed just 10 yards on nine carries, but his receiving role saved the day with 11 catches for 71 yards on 11 targets. Brown also handled more third-down work than usual and led the backfield in routes run. The rushing production was ugly, but this kind of workload keeps him firmly in the RB1 conversation. He gets a great matchup in Week 5 against a Dolphins defense that has allowed the most fantasy points per game to running backs.

Brian Thomas Jr. set season highs in snap rate and fantasy points (9.7), with a receiving touchdown helping his production against the Bengals. Jacksonville's increased use of 11 personnel also helped boost his playing time. Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers remain the top two receivers, but Thomas mixed into 12 personnel more than he had previously. His role is moving in the right direction, although he's still difficult to trust in fantasy lineups.

Brenton Strange set a season high in snaps and turned the expanded role into eight targets and 16.5 fantasy points, both season highs. Jacksonville's increased use of 11 personnel helped boost his playing time, while the favorable matchup against a Bengals defense that has allowed the fifth-most fantasy points per game to tight ends also contributed to the production.

Arizona Cardinals at New York Giants

Cam Skattebo is still the Giants' lead back and finished with 19 touches against the Cardinals, but the workload is becoming less concentrated. Tyrone Tracy Jr. handled most of the third-down snaps, while Najee Harris also rotated in on early downs. Skattebo's early-down involvement fell to a season low. He still led the Giants' backfield with 7.6 fantasy points, but averaged just 3.2 yards per carry.

Marvin Harrison Jr. finished with a season-high 8.2 fantasy points thanks to a receiving touchdown, but his playing time continues to trend down, and he set a season low in snaps against the Giants. Trey McBride (46) and Michael Wilson (44) have dominated Arizona's targets this season, while Harrison Jr. has just 13.

Los Angeles Rams at Philadelphia Eagles

Dontayvion Wicks had a chance to take on a bigger role with DeVonta Smith out, but it didn't lead to much fantasy production. He led Eagles pass catchers in snaps and routes but finished with just five targets and a season-low 4.8 fantasy points. Darius Cooper made more of his opportunity, finishing with season highs in targets (7) and fantasy points (18.3).

Green Bay Packers at Tampa Bay Buccaneers

The Packers leaned more heavily on 13 personnel against the Buccaneers, which helped Tucker Kraft stay on the field and finish with seven targets and 16.5 fantasy points. Matthew Golden also saw seven targets and scored 11.5 points. Christian Watson, meanwhile, saw his snaps dip to a season low and finished with just three targets and 7.7 fantasy points as Green Bay leaned more on 13 personnel.

Tennessee Titans at Baltimore Ravens

Carnell Tate finished with season highs in both targets (12) and fantasy points (21.5) against the Ravens. He led all Titans skill-position players in snaps, routes and targets. Tate's 145 receiving yards were the most in a game by a Titans rookie since A.J. Brown had 153 against the Raiders in 2019. Tate remains on the flex radar with upside in Week 5 against a Texans defense that has allowed the second-most fantasy points per game to wide receivers.

Tony Pollard continues to lead the Titans' backfield in touches this season, and that was the case again against the Ravens. He's had at least 18 touches and scored at least 13 fantasy points in back-to-back games. Pollard is firmly on the flex radar in Week 5 against a tough Texans matchup, then gets a more favorable spot in Week 6 against a Colts defense that has allowed the sixth-most fantasy points per game to running backs.

Dallas Cowboys at Houston Texans

The Texans changed the timing of their backfield rotation in Week 4. David Montgomery had typically handled the opening two possessions, but Woody Marks checked in on the second drive against the Cowboys. Montgomery still led the backfield in snaps and touches (10), but Marks finished with more fantasy points thanks to a rushing touchdown. Marks is also getting involved earlier in games and may be working his way into a larger weekly role.

Miami Dolphins at Minnesota Vikings

Ollie Gordon II may have moved to the top of the Dolphins backfield following De'Von Achane's season ending injury. Jaylen Wright started the game, but he struggled early as Miami rotated the backs by series. Gordon took over in the second half and finished the game leading the backfield in snaps, routes, touches (11) and fantasy points (18). He rushed for a career-high 100 yards.

Aaron Jones Sr. has continued to dominate snaps, routes and touches in the Vikings' backfield over the last three weeks with Jordan Mason on injured reserve. He finished with the second-most targets on the team (8), behind only T.J. Hockenson, who had 13. Jones also set a season high with 23 touches against the Dolphins and has scored at least 10 fantasy points in four straight games, including a season-high 16.8 in Week 4.

Kansas City Chiefs at Las Vegas Raiders

Kenneth Walker III has had at least 20 touches and scored at least 21 fantasy points in every game this season. However, Walker's route participation has dropped in each of the last two weeks. Walker has just three targets over that stretch after seeing 16 through the first two games. The production is still there, but the dip in passing-game work is worth watching.

Denver Broncos at San Francisco 49ers

George Kittle's playing time has increased each week, and that trend continued against the Broncos, when he played over 90% of the snaps. He's now scored at least 17 fantasy points in three straight games. Entering Monday, Kittle is the TE2 in fantasy and has been an excellent value relative to where he was drafted this summer.

Los Angeles Chargers at Seattle Seahawks

Omarion Hampton continues to disappoint because the Chargers are splitting the backfield almost evenly among three players. Hampton, Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal all played between 25 and 26 snaps on Sunday. Mitchell led the group with 15 touches, while Hampton had 11 and Vidal seven. Hampton scored a rushing touchdown and 13.3 fantasy points, Vidal had a receiving touchdown and 11.6, while Mitchell finished with 11.3. That kind of split puts a real cap on Hampton's weekly ceiling.

Detroit Lions at Carolina Panthers

Tetairoa McMillan scored 45.2 fantasy points against the Lions, the highest total by any player this season, with Jalen Coker and Xavier Legette sidelined. He led the Panthers in routes and targets, but the most interesting development was his production from the slot, where he was targeted heavily and generated nearly half of his fantasy points. It will be worth watching whether that usage continues once Coker and Legette return after Carolina's Week 5 bye.

Sam LaPorta finished with 13 targets and 22.4 fantasy points, leading the Lions in both categories as Detroit leaned heavily on the passing game. However, he ran the fourth-most routes among Lions pass catchers as his playing time in 11 personnel dipped. That's something to monitor if Detroit finds itself in more neutral or positive game scripts, although this defense has allowed the most yards and points per game to opponents.

stories.headline: Portugal, Man United, Real Madrid: Cristiano Ronaldo's long history of rows with coaches
stories.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo walked out of the Portugal national team's camp after being benched. It is far from the first high-profile row of his two decades at the top.
stories.body:
Editor's note: This has been updated after Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on the events that led to his departure from Portugal's team camp.

Was it always going to end like this? Cristiano Ronaldo -- Portugal's greatest-ever player, who led them to victory at the 2016 UEFA European Championship, and won the UEFA Champions League and the Ballon d'Or five times in a glittering club career -- walked away from the national team's camp on Wednesday, leaving his international future in doubt.

Ronaldo, 41, has since then spoken about the reasons for his departure. Days earlier, coach Jorge Jesus had insisted there was "no issue," but admitted mistakes in his handling of Ronaldo's role in Sunday's 2-1 win over Norway in the UEFA Nations League, where he was an unused substitute.

It is still unclear whether his departure means he has played his last game for Portugal. However, sources tell ESPN that Ronaldo has issued an ultimatum that he will not return to the national team while Jesus is the coach. But an acrimonious end to his international career -- during which he has scored a men's record 146 goals -- could hardly be described as a shock.

- Ronaldo goal tracker: 978 and counting on road to 1,000 career goals

- A kit fit for the GOAT: Messi's special kit for final Argentina match

- LaLiga unveils Clásico match ball for Barça vs. Real Madrid clashes

Managing the transition when an aging superstar's performance level drops is never easy, and Ronaldo's role and impact -- positive and negative -- with Portugal has been debated for three successive major tournaments now, in 2022, 2024 and 2026.

Throughout his 25-year career, Ronaldo has been involved in a series of headline-grabbing disagreements with managers, teammates and executives. As we wait for this latest drama to be resolved, here are some of the most high-profile previous examples.

Unhappy Ronaldo backs Blatter's insensitive "slavery" comparison (July 10, 2008)
Ronaldo's bid to leave Manchester United for Real Madrid that summer reached a new, histrionic high -- or low -- when Ronaldo echoed comments from then-FIFA president Sepp Blatter that keeping a player at a club against their will was comparable to "modern slavery." Ronaldo told Portugal's TV1: "It's true. I agree with what the president of FIFA said. I know what I want and what I would like. We have to see what happens. I do not know where I will begin next season." After five successful years at Old Trafford, Ronaldo was ready to move on, but United stood firm and the forward had to wait another season before his desired move to the Bernabéu was finally fulfilled.

Ronaldo subs himself off mid-game at Old Trafford (Dec. 6, 2008)
Ronaldo abruptly walked off the pitch -- and headed straight down the tunnel -- midway through Manchester United's 1-0 win over Sunderland at Old Trafford. The team were left playing with 10 men, as United's coaching staff rushed to organise an unexpected substitution. Manager Sir Alex Ferguson defended Ronaldo, saying he had received "a kick on the hip" and "there was no need for Cristiano to come to the bench" when he required immediate treatment, but it was clear that the player -- who had won his first Ballon d'Or earlier that week -- was increasingly willing to act out.

Derby withdrawal sparks bout of Ronaldo head-shaking (May 10, 2009)
Ronaldo's reaction to another substitution, this time in the heated atmosphere of a Manchester derby, was the latest sign of a growing estrangement between him and the club. He had put United ahead against City with an 18th-minute free kick -- the first goal of a 2-0 victory -- but when Ferguson opted to replace him with Paul Scholes on the hour, Ronaldo reacted furiously. He spent several minutes shaking his head in frustration on the bench in a very public, visible showing of discontent. That opening goal proved to be his last for the club for 12 years.

No celebrations for "sad" Ronaldo (Sept. 2, 2012)
Three years on from finally getting his desired move to Real Madrid, new signs of dissatisfaction emerged. Ronaldo had scored twice in a 3-0 LaLiga win over Granada, but was he happy? No, he wasn't. The lack of a goal celebration for either strike raised eyebrows, and his enigmatic postmatch comments set alarm bells ringing. "I'm sad because of a professional issue, and the club know it," Ronaldo revealed, mysteriously. "That's why I'm not celebrating my goals, because I'm not happy. The people here know why." The forward refused to elaborate, and an explanation for his ennui was never forthcoming. Ronaldo subsequently denied that money was the problem, but a bumper new contract that was eventually signed a year later might have helped.

Mourinho hits back at 'know-it-all' Ronaldo (June 5, 2013)
Ronaldo and manager José Mourinho were close when the two first worked together at Real Madrid, but -- in a developing trend -- their relationship was deteriorating by the end of the 2012-13 season, Mourinho's last at the Bernabéu. A dressing room bust-up after a Copa del Rey game with Valencia in January was the beginning of the end and by June, after dropping the forward for the last few games of the season, Mourinho was telling TV show Punto Pelota after leaving Los Blancos for a second spell at Chelsea that "Cristiano Ronaldo thinks he knows everything."

Ronaldo prefers Carlo to Rafa (Dec. 11, 2015)
Rafa Benítez was in charge at Real Madrid for only six months after replacing Carlo Ancelotti in June 2015 and getting sacked the next January, but there was still time for his relationship with Ronaldo to come under scrutiny. There was speculation that the player was unhappy with his manager's tactical approach, and Ronaldo's fulsome praise for predecessor Ancelotti -- calling him an "unbelievable person" and a "fantastic coach" (and, rather endearingly, a "big bear") whom he "wished to work with again" probably didn't help. Benítez insisted that he and the star were still "adapting to each other," but there wasn't time for that: A month later, Benítez was gone.

Ronaldo benched ahead of United move (Aug. 22, 2021)
Just a few days before the 2018 World Cup final (in which Portugal were not involved), Ronaldo's move to Juventus after nine years in Madrid was announced. But, after three years in Turin, Ronaldo was ready to move again. He was left out of the team for the Italian giants' Serie A opener for the 2021-22 season, a 2-2 draw at Udinese, after reportedly asking not to start the match. Juventus were insistent that the forward would stay, and Ronaldo himself had earlier branded reports linking him with a move back to Real Madrid as "disrespectful." However, just over a week later, he was on his way back to Manchester United on transfer deadline day having been heavily linked with joining rivals City.

Ronaldo is no fan of three at the back (Jan. 19, 2022)
If we've learned anything so far, it's that Ronaldo isn't keen on being substituted. Manchester United interim coach Ralf Rangnick found that out when looking to protect the team's 2-0 lead at Brentford by replacing Ronaldo with Harry Maguire and switching to a back three. Ronaldo wasn't a fan of the tactical change, throwing his coat to the ground as he departed, before Rangnick had to have a word. The reaction was "normal," Rangnick said, adding: "I said maybe when you're a head coach yourself you will hopefully make the same decision." The coach was proved right: United went on to win 3-1.

'Nonsense' reports of Maguire captaincy battle (Feb. 18, 2022)
A month later, Rangnick was called upon to dismiss claims of a rift between Ronaldo and defender Maguire as "absolute nonsense." The issue at stake was reportedly the United captaincy, with skipper Maguire feeling threatened by Ronaldo's outsized influence in the dressing room among younger players. Rangnick sought to quash that, saying, "I have never spoken with any player about a possible change of captaincy," and insisting Maguire would continue in his role until the end of the season.

Explosive interview forces Ronaldo's second Old Trafford exit (Nov. 13, 2022)
After a start to the season that saw Ronaldo's goals dry up and his first-team place rescinded by new manager Erik ten Hag, Ronaldo's clear frustration came to a head when on Oct. 21 when he refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham Hotspur, walked off down the tunnel and left Old Trafford before the final whistle -- something he also did during a preseason friendly with Rayo Vallecano.

His departure from United was finally sealed by a no-holds-barred interview with Piers Morgan. Ronaldo criticised just about everybody at Old Trafford -- saying he "didn't respect" Ten Hag, felt "betrayed" by senior executives, had "never heard of" Rangnick before his arrival and "zero progress" had been made since his first stint at the club. If the comprehensive takedown was designed to make his own position at United untenable, then it was a success, with the club agreeing to a departure by mutual agreement.

Ronaldo axed by Portugal, family reacts angrily (Dec. 6, 2022)
Ronaldo was dropped by coach Fernando Santos for Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 tie against Switzerland, and his replacement, Gonçalo Ramos, more than justified the decision, scoring a hat trick in a 6-1 win. Santos claimed the selection was based on "strategy," rather than Ronaldo's angry reaction to being substituted in Portugal's final group game, although Santos had previously said of his captain's outburst: "I didn't like it."

The Portuguese football federation (FPF) was then moved to deny reports that things had escalated before their quarterfinal against Morocco. "The FPF clarifies that at no time did the captain of the national team, Cristiano Ronaldo, threaten to leave the national team at any stage," it said in a statement.

Unsurprisingly, Ronaldo's omission didn't go well with the extended Ronaldo family. "What a shame not to have been able to enjoy the best player in the world for 90 minutes," partner Georgina Rodríguez said in a post on Instagram, and sister Elma Aveiro added: "It's a shame to humiliate a man who has given so much."

Ronaldo storms out of Portugal camp (Sept. 30, 2026)
And so here we are, waiting for Ronaldo to expand on the reasons for his latest walkout.

At the time of writing, we know that his exit followed a lack of minutes against Norway on Sunday, and then coach Jesus giving his version of events in a news conference three days later. Ronaldo, according to his own statement, then held "a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation." He also felt the need to wish his teammates "good luck, without exception" in Thursday's Nations League game with Denmark.

The last four years have been relatively calm by Ronaldo standards, with the forward scoring lots of goals -- and winning a couple of trophies -- with Al Nassr in the Saudi Pro League, and benefitting from a national team coach, Roberto Martínez, who backed him persistently at two major tournaments, despite growing criticism.

Jesus worked with Ronaldo at Al Nassr, but on this week's evidence, their relationship appears much less comfortable. We'll find out soon enough if it signals the end of a 23-year international career.

Ronaldo releases statement after Portugal matches (Oct. 6, 2026)
After Portugal's matches ended in the Nations League for the international window, Ronaldo released a statement about what happened behind the scenes between him and Portugal coach Jesus, and what his future holds with the team.

In his statement, he accused Jesus of breaking two promises. The first was that the coach told Ronaldo that he should be ready to play 30 minutes against Norway -- where Portugal won 2-1 in Oslo -- at lunchtime on the day of the match. Ronaldo ended up not playing.

The second was that Jesus had agreed to address the issue in the press conference on the day prior to their match against Denmark in Copenhagen, following private conversations between him and Ronaldo.

The points that were to be brought up in the news conference ranged from "wanting Cristiano on the national team" to admitting he "made a mistake in having someone of the stature of Pelé or [Diego] Maradona warm up and then not putting him into game."

Jesus later said in the conference that "every player knows the coach makes the decisions" and that Ronaldo told him he would abide by whatever choices he makes, adding that the "rules are the same for everyone."

After that, Ronaldo left the team camp, and Portugal ended up winning the next two matches without him in the squad. The statement continues by saying that he "apologizes to his national team teammates for having left the camp" and says that "the consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation."

He closes it by saying that he "promises to have one or more farewell matches" and that "he will be available, as I always have been until today, to compete and win for our national team."

Portugal's next matches are in November against Denmark and Wales to close out their Nations League group.

stories.headline: State of each position in 2026: What are the biggest tactical trends?
stories.summary: Elite soccer has changed dramatically in recent years, and the most valued player skill sets have evolved as a result.
stories.body:
Elite European soccer in 2026 feels decidedly different from what we've become used to. Over the past couple of seasons, the Premier League has been increasingly characterized by direct attacking, set pieces and long throw-ins. Many encounters between big clubs across Europe have become frenetic, end-to-end affairs, such as the Bayern Munich-Paris Saint-Germain semifinals in last season's UEFA Champions League.

A lot of the changes seem related to how teams play without the ball. The soccer we became accustomed to throughout the 2010s involved top sides trying to push their opponents back while keeping the ball. Once the ball reached the attacking third, they tried to outnumber defenders in key spaces and make use of their attacking talent.

One way for defensive sides to counter this approach is to use zonal marking, which involves defending space rather than individual players. They would set up in compact blocks and deny space in critical areas, whether they defended deep like Max Allegri's Juventus in the 2010s or pressed high like teams coached by Ralf Rangnick's disciples. While this tactic helps protect the areas closer to goal and prevent mismatches, it sometimes plays into the hands of those high-possession sides.

As a result, player marking (or man-to-man marking), in which defenders are assigned to follow attackers around up and down the pitch, started to make a comeback at the turn of the 2020s. Teams like Mikel Arteta's Arsenal and Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth combined this concept with their zonal marking, switching out of a zonal structure in certain situations to swarm teams attempting to move the ball forward (hybrid pressing). This makes moving the ball slowly up the pitch harder, causing teams to embrace more direct approaches with the ball.

Meanwhile, the game appears to be becoming more physical and more intense. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, every passing season of the Premier League has seen faster sprinting and more "high-intensity actions." And with off-ball physical data like running distance or top speed becoming more accessible, scouting departments now possess more transparent measures of athleticism, leading to players' athletic qualities being valued more.

Rather than just affecting the head coach's team talk, these big-picture changes have a major effect on the skill sets that clubs look for when assembling their starting XIs. Let's take a look at five positions -- goalkeepers, center backs, fullbacks, central midfielders, and strikers -- to see what has changed and why.

Goalkeepers: Distribution and cross-claiming

New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki has generated much buzz this season. One of his standout features has been his passing ability, playing quick passes to his center backs during the early buildup and exquisite floated long passes to Villa's forwards to escape pressure.

As impressive as his reflex saves are, Suzuki doesn't appear to be a great shot stopper. His "goals prevented" stats, based on post-shot expected goals, reveal that his shot-stopping numbers have hovered around that of the average major league goalkeeper over the past couple of seasons. In fact, in 2025-26, he prevented minus-0.4 goals per 90 minutes, implying that he did slightly worse than the average keeper last season.

However, his passing displays and his excellent cross-claiming make him a highly prized player, and his skill set epitomizes the state of today's goalkeeping.

When Pep Guardiola's Manchester City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma -- known for his shot-stopping abilities, but arguably an average distributor -- as their first-choice goalkeeper in summer 2025, it looked like elite soccer was once again prioritizing shot-stopping between the sticks. But the tactical conditions of soccer in the 2020s make ball-playing goalkeepers even more crucial than before; when teams are tasked with playing the ball past intense man-to-man presses, goalkeepers have more to do in the buildup phase.

Even the most aggressive man-to-man presses don't generally mark the goalkeeper, making keepers free options in the buildup. From this point, keepers are instrumental to playing quick passes around the box to try to bait the press for "artificial transitions" as well as with playing longer passes into space to relieve pressure and kick-start a direct attack.

As a result, the heyday of keepers primarily known for what they can do with their feet looks unlikely to recede anytime soon, with more intense pressing and more direct attacking arguably magnifying their value.

Meanwhile, although the number of open-play crosses that teams in the Big Five leagues play has decreased slightly since 2018, the ever-rising threat of set-play goals makes cross-claiming an especially valuable skill. The first-choice keepers at big clubs dominate the top of the leaderboard for cross-claiming statistics; Donnarumma ranked No. 1 for the highest percentage of crosses claimed in the Premier League last season, Barcelona's Joan García and Real Madrid's Thibaut Courtois ranked second and third, respectively, in last season's LaLiga campaign, and PSG's Lucas Chevalier ranked third in Ligue 1.

On the other hand, the keepers who populated the bottom of cross-claiming tables belong to either lower-table clubs or underperforming established sides like Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United. As valuable as goalkeepers' distribution is in 2026, it appears that the ability to claim crosses has become crucial to success between the sticks.

Center backs: Playmaking and pushing forward

In the 2015-16 Premier League season, the top five players who completed the most passes per 90 were Santi Cazorla, Cesc Fabregas, Bastian Schweinsteiger, Aaron Ramsey and Michael Carrick, with more central and attacking midfielders completing the top 10. In 2025-26, the top five were Rodri, Lewis Dunk, Curtis Jones, Trevoh Chalobah and William Saliba, with seven center backs making up the top 10.

A decade ago, central midfielders were at the heart of elite sides' passing moves, but today, especially in the Premier League, center backs are the primary passers in most sides.

In the Big Five leagues, center backs completed 19% more passes in the 2025-26 season than in 2018-19. Much of this has to do with intense man-to-man pressing systems, meaning that players positioned deeper have more prominent buildup duties. The 2020s have also seen nominal center backs become more involved in attacking play, taking up higher and wider positions. Attacking center backs are effective tools to dismantle mid-blocks, helping complicate marking duties with their movement.

This is easiest to do with wide center backs in a back three. Gian Piero Gasperini's Atalanta and Simone Inzaghi's Internazionale did this especially often. This season, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea and Gasperini's AS Roma are key examples, with the latter probably representing the most adventurous iteration of attacking center backs we've seen this century.

We can see some of this in back-four systems, too. Guardiola used John Stones as a center back who roved forward in possession at City, while Thiago Motta used Riccardo Calafiori and Jhon Lucumí as center backs with free roles.

As this decade progresses, the phrase "center back" might be encased in quotation marks more often.

Fullbacks: Rise of the underlap

Fullbacks often epitomize the tactical eras they find themselves in. The turn of the 2010s saw the rise of overlapping attacking fullbacks who move high up the pitch and outside wingers who cut inside with the ball. The mid-to-late 2010s saw the rise of high-intensity pressing, with high-possession sides using inverted fullbacks to provide security against counterattacks resulting from losing the ball. Meanwhile, the relative conservatism that followed the COVID-19 pandemic meant that nominal center backs were often deployed at fullback.

Today, we're seeing the rise of attacking fullbacks who underlap, making runs into the channels between opposition fullbacks and center backs, much like inverted wingers. As Caleb Gearty notes for SCOUTED, "the ability to receive the ball" is progressively becoming more highly valued for fullbacks. After getting in behind back lines, underlapping fullbacks can put in dangerous cutbacks and crosses from closer to goal, or take shots themselves.

In the case of back-three formations, this isn't a new phenomenon. For instance, Thomas Tuchel's Chelsea saw wingbacks Reece James and Ben Chilwell move inside and score goals, while Inzaghi used Federico Dimarco and Denzel Dumfries as goal-scoring threats at Inter.

But now, fullbacks in back-four systems are increasingly venturing forward and inside -- not just putting crosses in, but getting on the end of goal-scoring opportunities, too. Arsenal's Calafiori and Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly often make darting runs into the box and offer secondary goal threats. Spain's World Cup win saw Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro underlap, pulling defenses apart.

Meanwhile, back-three systems feature wingbacks who pose greater goal-scoring threats than ever. Alonso's Chelsea are an instructive example -- they signed Pep Chavarría and Marco Palestra, but Alonso currently appears to favor the left-footed winger Pedro Neto at right wingback, who makes sharp runs into the box.

Why is this the case? In an age when defensive tactics are dominated by player-marking, the positional interchanges around the flanks (or "wide rotations") and unexpected diagonal darts forward from fullbacks can scramble player-marking duties and open up space -- especially when wingers find themselves closer to the sideline. As Billy Carpenter writes, sudden moves into the spaces in behind defenses can expose structural vulnerabilities in even the best mid-blocks.

Calafiori so far this season represents a great example, making well-timed runs in behind and receiving incisive through balls ...

... and creating goals like these.

Jamie Carragher once remarked that fullbacks are either failed wingers or failed center backs. The rise of inverted fullbacks would've allowed Carragher to add "failed midfielder" to his jibe, while today, a middling inside forward can consider a successful career as an underlapping attacking fullback.

Central midfielders: Large spaces and generalists

In 2026, the most expensive player archetype to sign in soccer appears to be the generalist midfielder. Of the 10 most expensive transfers this summer per Transfermarkt, six were central midfielders. And among the major moves in midfield that big clubs made this summer, most midfielders are do-it-all generalists who, at least in theory, contribute to passing, carrying, winning the ball back and sometimes crashing the box. These include Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Bruno Guimarães, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

This hasn't always been the case. By 2009, the box-to-box midfielder had become a dying breed, superseded by specialists in midfield. In the late 2010s, the rise of pressing meant that press-resistant ball carriers in midfield became increasingly valued, epitomized by the summer 2019 transfer window, which saw Frenkie de Jong, Tanguy Ndombele and Mateo Kovacic move for sums exceeding €40 million. But now, every big club is willing to spend astronomic sums on their own equivalent of Declan Rice or Moisés Caicedo; athletic midfielders who can cover lots of ground and do a bit of everything.

Counterintuitively, this might be happening because less of the game is happening in midfield. With the rise of situational player-marking, the middle third sees larger spaces opened up between lines of pressure, while space becomes more constricted in teams' own thirds. As a result, moving the ball from defense to midfield becomes a harder task, while the spaces opened up in the middle third mean teams don't pass the ball around as much there, instead moving the ball through it more quickly.

Jon Mackenzie and Jake Entwistle have discussed the relevance of "small spaces" -- where the player on the ball has little room to work with in the face of pressure -- and "large spaces" -- where players need to cover ground quickly, especially during transitions or when a line of pressure is broken -- in midfield, which influences how midfielder profiles are valued today. A player like Anderson, who combines small-space and large-space skills, becomes priceless, but the broader emphasis shifts from small-space specialists to large-space generalists who can cover ground and offer control in the center of the park.

As a result, affecting the pace of the attack, rather than just exerting control over space, becomes a key consideration in midfield. The rise of artificial transitions in response to pressing also means central midfielders are key to moving the ball from small spaces to large spaces, as Carlos Baleba did adeptly while at Brighton.

The middle of the park is integral to controlling a game of soccer, and as we're seeing the very notion of "control" change in the middle of the 2020s, the traits associated with the most highly valued midfielders are transformed, too.

Strikers: Physicality and pinning

While the first two decades of top-level soccer in the 21st century saw increasing versatility at the center forward position, the opposite is happening in the third decade. So far, the 2020s have seen taller, faster and stronger strikers being valued more than their smaller, more technical counterparts. Of course, Erling Haaland represents the platonic ideal of a striker -- in this era and in any other -- but the players who spearhead attacks in the middle of the 2020s tend to be 6-foot-2 or taller, and combine their size with pace.

Today's strikers are also less involved in link-up play than their equivalents at the turn of the 2020s, with the average striker in the Big Five leagues completing 16% fewer passes in 2025-26 than in 2018-19.

As discussed earlier, with attacks becoming more direct, the established strategy of pushing teams back and overwhelming defenses with patient play in the attacking third is falling out of fashion, which means strikers don't need to be as involved outside the penalty area. Instead, strikers increasingly spend most of the game pinning back defenders and stretching back lines, attempting to find space within settled defensive blocks. Plus, an increased emphasis on transitions correspondingly makes outlets to hit on the break becoming more valuable, and some extra size certainly comes in handy while trying to score goals from set pieces.

However, the players who currently lead most big clubs' front lines indicate the trend might be reversing at the upper echelons of the game. Harry Kane drops deeper than ever and conducts passing moves from midfield at Bayern, PSG won the Champions League with Ousmane Dembélé as a false 9 last season, Mikel Arteta appears to favor Kai Havertz up front over Viktor Gyokeres at Arsenal, and Barcelona currently deploy Raphinha at the No. 9 spot.

This might be because teams are finding alternate ways of manipulating player-marking strategies, picking holes in defenses with positional interchanges. By dropping deeper, a striker can bring the defender assigned to marking him along and create space for teammates. For example, in this case, João Pedro dropping deep to receive a throw-in pokes a hole for Morgan Rogers to run into, who in turn creates space for Cole Palmer's carry and goal.

For now, specialized, physically gifted strikers may have their time in the sun, but we're likely to see many approaches at the center forward position as the decade progresses.

What to make of 2026 trends

Many soccer fans view today's tactical landscape as being one of stasis or even regression. It's tempting to view the rise of directness and set pieces, as well as do-it-all midfielders and big strikers, as the return of older approaches. But this might be a reductive view; as Mackenzie notes in his book "The Spectre of Pep," presenting changes in the tactical landscape as purely being "cyclical" makes it "very difficult to speak of the 'new' in any meaningful way at all."

All the smaller tactical shifts we're seeing across the pitch are happening in relation to broader changes in the tactical environment of the 2020s. With the rise of man-to-man pressing approaches and the resulting revival of direct attacking, accompanied with the resurgence of ground-eating midfielders and big, physical strikers, these very same trends have brought about the rise of playmaking goalkeepers, attacking center backs, and underlapping fullbacks.

If a Premier League manager from 2006 drove a plutonium-powered DeLorean to 2026, he might find the first five minutes of play recognizable, but would be scandalized by the time he reaches the 10-minute mark. Welcome to elite soccer in the 2020s.

stories.headline: What's next: Will Silva's first title defense be against Shevchenko?
stories.summary: The most likely opponent and a wild card for the winners and losers on the UFC 332 main card.
stories.body:
The UFC has a new women's flyweight champion for the first time in over two years following the UFC 332 main event in Salt Lake City on Saturday night. And with a new champion comes brand-new matchups. After winning the belt via unanimous decision over Wang Cong, Natalia Silva will have no shortage of challengers looking for their shot at gold.

Also on the UFC 332 fight card, rising men's bantamweight contender Payton Talbott made quick work of former two-time men's flyweight champion Deiveson Figueiredo in the co-main event. Talbott could take on a top-ranked contender in his next Octagon appearance. And a handful of young prospects earned impressive first-round knockout victories.

Here's what's next for the top stars of UFC 332.

Natalia Silva, women's flyweight champion

Who should be next: Valentina Shevchenko

The state of the UFC's women's divisions is not ideal. We haven't seen a bantamweight title fight all year, due to injuries to Kayla Harrison. Mackenzie Dern is the strawweight champion, but (fair or not) there is a pretty significant need for her to fight Zhang Weili to validate her standing as the top 115-pound fighter in the world, since Zhang vacated her belt, never lost it in competition. Now the same is true of the flyweight title. Silva has the longest active win streak at 125 pounds and might be the best in the world, but she'll battle for that perception until she fights Shevchenko. We'll have to see how long Shevchenko is out, but this fight needs to happen as soon as possible.

Wild card: Erin Blanchfield

Blanchfield has looked like future champion material since she debuted with the UFC at 22 years old in 2021. She's now five years into her UFC career, and she is 8-1 with one learning experience in the form of a five-round decision loss to Manon Fiorot in 2024. She's still only 27 and could well prove to be the future of this weight class. She's got a tough matchup scheduled against Jasmine Jasudavicius on Oct. 17. If she gets past that unscathed, the UFC could easily book her with Silva as soon as possible, instead of waiting for Shevchenko.

Payton Talbott, men's bantamweight
Who should be next: Sean O'Malley

It has to be done. O'Malley was once the darling of the bantamweight division. Now it's Talbott, and it's hard to deny this matchup. Now, the UFC is almost certainly already looking at O'Malley for an upcoming title fight. Especially if Petr Yan defeats Merab Dvalishvili at UFC 333 later this month, O'Malley is the favorite to face Yan next. But if UFC fans were polled, the more anticipated fight might honestly be O'Malley vs. Talbott. Not to get out of control here, but this could headline a numbered event.

Wild card: Farid Basharat

This would be the anti-O'Malley booking. The UFC doesn't love that Basharat has mostly decisions on his record -- so much so that there's been some uncertainty about his security with the promotion. He's ranked in the top 10 by the UFC but in a spot to defend his spot (not attack). This is the kind of athlete who might need to fight down the rankings. Enter Talbott.

Ateba Gautier, middleweight
Who should be next: Loser of Bo Nickal vs. Joe Pyfer on Dec. 12

Hear me out: Gautier's hype train took a major, major hit with the first-round knockout loss to Roman Kopylov. There's no way around it. He took a step up in competition, and fell very flat. In this situation, the UFC can quietly step him back to the prelims somewhere -- or it can create a story. Gautier's stock took a hit but he is still extremely dangerous. There's still intrigue attached to him. Nickal is coming off a strong win at the White House over Kyle Daukaus, but there are still question marks around him. Pyfer is riding high after a finish of Israel Adesanya in his last bout. Whoever loses between Nickal and Pyfer would still be in position for a compelling bout. What's more compelling than this? There is still a way for the UFC to use what's left of the hype around Gautier and make a fight fans will want to watch.

Wild card: Loser of Daukaus vs. Marc-Andre Barriault on Oct. 17

This would be an appropriate next step that would teach us more about Gautier. Kopylov is a legitimate (for lack of a better word) gatekeeper, and Daukaus and Andre Barriault are also proven veterans. Either would challenge Gautier and offer him a chance at redemption.

stories.headline: Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.
stories.body:
Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.

It will also be the sixth and final sprint race of the season as Singapore hosts it for the first time.

Max Verstappen claimed his first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, while Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the title championship to 84 points from George Russell.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 17th round of the season.

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play despite Sepang travel chaos

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

Singapore Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Friday, October 9

Practice One: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Sprint Qualifying: 1.30 p.m. - 2.14 p.m.

Saturday, October 10

Sprint: 10 a.m. - 11 a.m.

Qualifying: 2 p.m. - 3 p.m.

Sunday, October 11

Singapore Grand Prix: 1 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Singapore Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Marina Bay Street Circuit

Singapore is one of the toughest challenges on the calendar for drivers due to the intense humidity and physically demanding nature of the circuit.

But this time round the drivers will have had a chance to get used to the humid conditions after racing in Malaysia for the Bahrain Grand Prix last weekend.

The Marina Bay Circuit has been on the calendar since 2008 and is one of the standout tracks. The race takes place at night with its breathtaking views of the city's skyline as cars make their way through the tight and twisty circuit.

Drivers can lose around 3kg in body weight after each race due to the amount they sweat.

Singapore Grand Prix

Circuit: Marina Bay Street Circuit; Singapore

Previous winners in Singapore

2014: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2015: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2016: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2017: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2022: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2023: Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2024: Lando Norris (McLaren)

2025: George Russell (Mercedes)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2008

Lap record: 1:33.808 Lewis Hamilton (2025)

Most wins: Sebastian Vettel has the most wins with five (2011-2013, 2015 and 2019). From the current grid, Hamilton has four wins (2009, 2014, 2017-2018) and Fernando Alonso with two (2008 and 2010). Pérez (2022), Sainz (2023), Norris (2024) and Russell (2025) have all won a race each here.

Most poles: Vettel (2011, 2013, 2015, 2017) and Hamilton (2009, 2012, 2014, 2018) share the pole record with four each. From the current grid, Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022) has had two pole positions here.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Singapore Grand Prix is set to be thundery showers and light winds throughout the weekend, with highs of 34°C on Friday. The temperature is forecast to drop a degree for the remainder of the weekend.

What happened last time out?
Russell claimed pole position in Singapore last year and crossed the line 0.182 seconds clear of Red Bull's Verstappen, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri behind.

Russell took his second win of the season, but there was plenty of other drama during the race, especially at McLaren.

Norris, who started in fifth, knocked into Piastri when trying to pass him in the first corner. Piastri managed to gain some ground towards the end of the race, but he had to settle for fourth on the day McLaren lifted the trophy for the constructors' title.

Piastri's drivers' championship lead to Norris was separated by only 22 points with six races left of the season.

Who will win this year?

One to watch this weekend is Red Bull and Verstappen after he won the race last weekend. The team brought major upgrades two races ago and improvements to its overall performance has been evident.

Russell, who suffered a major blow to his championship hopes after retiring last time out, will be looking to maximise the points on offer across the weekend.

Mercedes are expected to be strong, while Ferrari are quick in cornering speed. Hamilton has won four times here, so could be a threat. McLaren's Norris and Piastri fell under the radar and struggled for pace in Malaysia.

All will be to play for under the lights in Singapore as we head into the business end of the season.

stories.headline: USMNT's young stars shine to give Pochettino 'fantastic problem'
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.
stories.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. -- United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.

The U.S. endured a difficult first half, and scored completely against the run of play in the 28th minute when Hall converted from close range after Mexico keeper Raúl Rangel spilled Gio Reyna's low cross right in front of goal.

- Cavan Sullivan has arrived: U.S. phenom's goal caps a memorable win over Mexico

- Márquez bemoans 'terrible mistakes' as Mexico humbled by USMNT

- USMNT player ratings: Sullivan, Hall 9/10 in big win vs. Mexico

The USMNT began to make more headway in the second half, and doubled its lead in the 62nd minute when Sullivan intercepted a pass from Rangel, and chipped the ball into the net from 35 yards out. The match lost its edge when Mexico's Mateo Chávez was red carded in the 67th minute following a scrap with Sebastian Berhalter.

Malik Tillman finished off the scoring in the 84th minute, latching onto another wayward Mexico pass to firing into the net.

Hall, 18, is just the third USMNT player to score in his first three national team appearances, while 17-year-old Sullivan became the youngest scorer in USMNT history.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino said about the performances of his team's young players. "I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and of course hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Pochettino also pronounced himself pleased with the way his side weathered Mexico's early pressure.

"I think that this, overall, was a great opportunity to discover ourself, to see ourselves in a difficult game with a very good team. Again, Mexico is a great team," Pochettino said.

"Yes, I think two different maybe halves. The first half I think Mexico started really well. They forced us to play back. We never connected. We were losing all the duels. And then we start to grow after 15, 20 minutes. And I think it was a good lesson the first half because it was the sense of work all together, suffer together even when you are not playing well in the way that you plan to play."

But Pochettino couldn't help but admire the performance of Sullivan, who impressed with his work on both sides the ball.

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said about Sullivan. "He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous quality.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he need to be chasing people and recover the ball. That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this. I think it's a fantastic news for USA. Hope that continues in that way."

Pochettino was careful to laud Sullivan's young teammates as well, who have largely impressed during this window.

"It's a big moment because we need to be right with them," Pochettino said about the win, and the path forward. "We need to protect them. We need to support them. Our responsibility now is that this group of talented players grow in the right direction."

stories.headline: Uncapped NRL trio picked in England's World Cup squad
stories.summary: Ben Talty, Hugo Savala and Max King headline a new-look England squad for the Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Brisbane prop Ben Talty, Canterbury front-rower Max King and Sydney Roosters utility Hugo Savala have been named in England's Rugby League World Cup squad.

Talty and Savala both qualify through ancestry and join Huddersfield-born King in a side assembled by Brian McDermott which contains 10 NRL players.

Savala's Roosters teammate Victor Radley is included along with Newcastle winger Dominic Young and the Dolphins duo of Morgan Knowles and Herbie Farnworth.

Canberra's Perth-bound prop Morgan Smithies has earned selection along with Wests Tigers backrower Kai Pearce-Paul and Gold Coast fullback AJ Brimson, who debuted for England in last year's Ashes whitewash.

McDermott, who is an assistant at the Titans and previously won the Super League title with Leeds, has taken over from Shaun Wane since the 3-0 series defeat.

Leeds halfback Jake Connor -- winner of last year's Man of Steel and controversially left out of the 2025 Ashes -- has again missed the cut, with McDermott preferring Hull KR playmaker Mikey Lewis.

McDermott said: "We have selected the squad after a thorough and deliberate process, underpinned by a unique decentralised preparation model that has allowed us to work closely with the players well before they come together in camp.

"Throughout that process, we have challenged players to develop a deeper understanding of themselves - their strengths, their point of difference, the areas they need to improve and the standards required to perform at international level."

England will kick off against Tonga on October 17 before also facing France and Papua New Guinea in the group stage.

England squad: Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Ben Currie, Zach Eckersley, Herbie Farnworth, Ethan Havard, Max King, Morgan Knowles, Mikey Lewis, Jez Litten, Junior Nsemba, Brad O'Neill, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley, Hugo Savala, Harry Smith, Morgan Smithies, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Ben Talty, Jack Welsby, George Williams, Dom Young.
